nodes.title: Real coefficient Schur series
nodes.statement: A real coefficient sequence e : ℕ → ℝ is a real Schur series when there exists f : ℂ → ℂ holomorphic on |z|<1 such that Σ e_j z^j converges to f(z) at every point of that disc and |f(z)|≤1 there. The function is uniquely determined on the disc; no boundary extension is required. The formal series is PowerSeries.mk e.
hypotheses: The disc is open. Real coefficients are part of the object, rather than a reality assumption on f at every complex point.
proofSteps: Use HasSum for the coefficient expansion and DifferentiableOn for holomorphy; uniqueness of sums makes the associated function independent of its witness.
Conjugating the expansion gives f(conj z)=conj(f(z)); polynomial and rational examples use the existing Cauchy power-series API.

sources.match: The coefficient estimates apply to real-coefficient bounded holomorphic functions; this definition removes the unnecessary neighbourhood-of-the-closed-disc restriction.

acceptance: The closed bound permits constant functions ±1, while every nonconstant witness maps into the open disc.

nodes.title: Smyth’s bounded holomorphic quotient
nodes.statement: Let P∈ℤ[X] be monic, P(0)=±1, with no complex root on the unit circle. Put Q=P.reverse and A=M(P). There are real-coefficient finite Blaschke products f,g, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disc, with f(0)=g(0)=c=A⁻¹>0 and Q(z)f(z)=P(0)P(z)g(z). On points where Q and g are nonzero, f/g=P(0)P/Q. If P is irreducible and nonreciprocal, that quotient is nonconstant and not a polynomial.
hypotheses: P(0)=±1 excludes zero roots; no roots on the unit circle is explicit.
Irreducibility and nonreciprocity are used only for the final non-polynomial assertion.
proofSteps: Use b_α for roots α of P inside the disc to form f, and b_(α⁻¹) for roots α of P outside the disc to form g, with multiplicities.

The inside-root product and the inverse outside-root product both have absolute value A⁻¹ because the total root product has modulus 1. Conjugation-stability makes the products real-coefficient; choose real signs to make both constants positive.

Compare the two rational functions by their zeros and poles and their value at zero. In the irreducible nonreciprocal case P and Q are coprime and have equal degree, so their nonconstant quotient is not polynomial.

sources.match: The two bounded root products have the same positive constant, the inverse Mahler measure.

acceptance: Keep the cross-multiplied identity; dividing at a zero of g is not permitted.

nodes.title: Schur’s first and doubled-index coefficient conditions
nodes.statement: If e is a real Schur series, c=e_0 and k≥1, then |e_k|≤1−c². If |c|<1, also −(1−c²)+e_k²/(1+c) ≤ e_(2k) ≤ (1−c²)−e_k²/(1−c). For c=±1 all coefficients of positive index vanish; the fractional inequalities are not stated there.
hypotheses: e real Schur; k≥1. The doubled-index inequalities require |c|<1.
proofSteps: Average the witness over kth-root rotations. The resulting bounded function has expansion h(w)=c+e_k w+e_(2k)w²+⋯; existence on the disc follows from the rotation-invariant series.

For |c|<1 apply the disc automorphism to h and divide by w: s(w)=(h(w)−c)/(w(1−c h(w))). Schwarz’s lemma makes s a disc map. Its first two coefficients are e_k/(1−c²) and e_(2k)/(1−c²)+c e_k²/(1−c²)².

Schwarz–Pick at zero bounds the derivative of s. A boundary value |s(0)|=1 forces s constant by the maximum principle, giving the same non-strict bounds. Rearrange to the two displayed inequalities. Treat c=±1 by the maximum principle on the original witness.

sources.match: The lemma bounds every positive coefficient and relates the kth and doubled-index coefficients. The Schur-transform proof here also applies without a boundary extension.

acceptance: For (c+z^k)/(1+c z^k), the upper doubled-index bound is attained: e_k=1−c² and e_(2k)=−c(1−c²).
For −1<c<1 both denominators are positive; no multiplication by an unknown-sign denominator is used.

nodes.title: Finite Parseval inequalities for Schur coefficients
nodes.statement: Let e be a real Schur series, p a finitely supported complex sequence, and N∈ℕ. Then Σ_(m=0)^N |Σ_(j=0)^m p_j e_(m−j)|² ≤ Σ_j |p_j|². In particular any selected finite set of output coefficients gives a lower bound for the squared norm of the input polynomial.
hypotheses: The input sum on the right is finite. The output is a finite initial truncation or any finite subset.
proofSteps: On the circle of radius r<1 the holomorphic product f(z)Σ p_j z^j is continuous and square integrable. Identify its Fourier coefficients from its absolutely convergent Taylor expansion.
Apply the pinned Parseval identity with period 2π and bound |f|≤1. The output terms carry r^(2m), while the input terms carry r^(2j).
Let r tend to 1 from below in the finite output and finite input sums. Nonnegative omitted terms justify replacing the full output sum by the chosen finite subset.

sources.match: Parseval after multiplication by two- and three-term polynomials is the analytic mechanism for the coefficient inequalities.

acceptance: For f=z^k the complete output norm equals the input norm; the 2π normalization must cancel.
The estimate does not assert a boundary value of an arbitrary Schur witness.

nodes.title: The first two nonzero integral quotient coefficients
nodes.statement: Let f,g have real Schur coefficient sequences u,v with u_0=v_0=c, 3/4≤c<1, and F∈ℤ⟦z⟧ satisfy F_0=1 and Fg=f. Suppose F is not a polynomial. Let 0<k<l be its first two nonzero positive indices, with coefficients a_k,a_l. Then |a_k|=|a_l|=1, |u_k|+|v_k|=c, and c/2≤1−c². Coefficient coupling gives u_k−v_k=a_k c, u_(k+i)−v_(k+i)=a_k v_i for 0<i<l−k, and u_l−v_l=a_k v_(l−k)+a_l c.
hypotheses: F non-polynomial ensures two positive nonzero coefficients exist; it is stronger than merely nonconstant.
All equalities are formal coefficient equalities and require no division at a zero of g.
proofSteps: Choose the first two nonzero indices using well-ordering and the non-polynomial hypothesis; apply the pinned finite coefficient convolution to Fg=f.
The Schur coefficient bound gives |a_k|c≤2(1−c²). Since c≥3/4, the integer |a_k| cannot be ≥2.
Because 1−c²<c, u_k and v_k have opposite signs, giving the absolute-value sum. At index l, |a_l|c≤3(1−c²)<2c, which rules out |a_l|≥2.
The larger of |u_k| and |v_k| is at least c/2, giving the weak quadratic condition.

sources.match: The integer quotient coefficients and the Schur bounds force the two first nonzero coefficients to be signs and the kth coefficients to have opposite signs.

acceptance: The k<l<2k branch gives u_(l−k)=v_(l−k); the long-gap branch uses the doubled-index coupling instead.

nodes.title: The cubic condition in Smyth’s long-gap case
nodes.statement: Under the preceding Schur-pair assumptions, if F has no positive nonzero coefficient between k and 2k inclusive, then c³+c²≤1. If the second nonzero index equals 2k, replacing F by F⁻¹ and interchanging the Schur pair produces the same case after ruling out a coefficient of magnitude 2.
hypotheses: 3/4≤c<1, |a_k|=1, F_(2k)=0 in the normalized case.
proofSteps: Put S=1−c². For a_k=1 write x=u_k≥0 and v_k=x−c≤0; then c−S≤x≤S and u_(2k)−v_(2k)=x−c.

The lower Schur bound for u_(2k) and upper bound for v_(2k) give J(x)=x²/(1+c)+(c−x)²/(1−c)+(c−x)≤2S. For a_k=−1 the same expression follows by replacing the positive-coefficient variable by its complementary value c−x.
J is decreasing on [c−S,S]: its derivative has numerator at most 3−5c²−2c<0 for c≥3/4. Thus J(S)≤2S. The identity J(S)−2S=(c³+c²−1)/(1−c) proves the conclusion.

When l=2k, the inverse quotient has coefficient a_k²−a_(2k)=1−a_(2k). The value 2 contradicts the reduction bound at its second nonzero coefficient; the value 0 gives the normalized long-gap case. Do not swap a second time just to set a_k=1, since this would restore a_(2k)=1.

sources.match: The doubled-index coefficient restrictions give the cubic condition after a one-variable minimization.

acceptance: The exact endpoint identity uses 1−c>0.
The sign a_k=−1 is included; normalizing l>2k and then swapping again would invalidate the normalization.

nodes.title: The quartic condition in Smyth’s short-gap case
nodes.statement: Let f,g be the bounded real-coefficient products in the Schur reduction. Assume 3/4≤c<(√17−1)/4 and k<l<2k. Then 40c⁴−93c²+40≥0. Consequently c³+c²<1 on this interval, equivalently c⁻¹>θ₀.
hypotheses: The strict upper endpoint is the reciprocal of (1+√17)/4. Its arithmetic justification is supplied separately.
This node records the exact source-supported target; its weighted three-term multiplier verification is named in gaps.
proofSteps: Interchange the quotient and pair to set a_k=1; because l<2k the second coefficient remains a sign and its index remains l.

Apply the finite Parseval contract to the two three-term multipliers in Smyth §4. Use u_(l−k)=v_(l−k), the couplings at k and l, and x=−a_l u_(l−k). The precise multiplier and selected-coefficient inequality must be checked from the displayed equations, not inferred from OCR.
Eliminate the two multiplier parameters by completing squares; minimize the resulting positive quadratic in x. The final necessary condition is 40c⁴−93c²+40≥0 (Smyth p. 173).

For A=c⁻¹∈((1+√17)/4,4/3], this is A⁴−(93/40)A²+1≥0. That polynomial is increasing on this interval and at θ₀ equals θ₀²(θ₀−53/40)<0. The last strict sign follows by evaluating T³−T−1 at 53/40, rather than using a decimal approximation.

sources.locator: §4, pp. 172–174, final quartic condition on p. 173
sources.match: The first gap smaller than k forces the stated quartic condition, which excludes the plastic threshold. Intermediate displayed multiplier formulas are not legible in the obtained extraction.

acceptance: At c=θ₀⁻¹ the quartic is negative; at c=3/4 it is positive. Both are useful signs for the elimination.

nodes.title: Integrality of the Mahler measure of a monic integer polynomial
nodes.statement: For a monic P∈ℤ[X], M(P), regarded as a real algebraic number, is integral over ℤ. In the Schur reduction for an irreducible nonreciprocal P with M(P)≤4/3, the weak bound M(P)≥(1+√17)/4 is therefore strict.
hypotheses: P monic. The strict-bound consequence also assumes the preceding Schur reduction.
proofSteps: Every complex root α is integral, as is its complex conjugate because P has real coefficients. Thus |α|²=α·conj(α) is integral; integrality of a positive power implies integrality of |α| in ℂ. Reflect integrality along ℝ→ℂ.
The root-product formula expresses M(P) as a finite product of 1 and |α|, hence as an integral element.
The quadratic number (1+√17)/4 has irreducible primitive polynomial 2T²−T−2 and field trace 1/2; it is not integral. Use this exclusion after the weak coefficient bound.

sources.locator: §3, p. 172, strictness after the first quadratic bound
sources.match: The first bound is strict because a Mahler measure is integral but the quadratic endpoint is not.

acceptance: The claim is for monic integer P; it is not asserted for arbitrary complex polynomials.

nodes.title: The analytic input for Smyth’s theorem
nodes.statement: Let P∈ℤ[X] be monic irreducible, P(0)=±1, P.reverse≠±P, and M(P)≤4/3. Then M(P)³−M(P)−1≥0. This supplies the missing analytic dependency of CA.6/smyth-nonreciprocal-lower-bound; the parent’s reductions for non-units and the plastic-number certificate remain its arithmetic dependencies.
hypotheses: Positive degree, irreducibility and nonreciprocity exclude unit-circle roots: conjugation followed by inversion would otherwise make P reciprocal.
proofSteps: Use the bounded factorization and the integral quotient from the parent. Their common positive constant c=M(P)⁻¹ lies in [3/4,1); if c=1, the positive Schur coefficients vanish and F is constant.
The first-coefficient reduction and monic Mahler integrality give c<(√17−1)/4.
For k<l<2k use the short-gap quartic condition and its strict comparison with θ₀. For l≥2k use the inverse-series normalization and the long-gap cubic condition.
Translate c³+c²≤1 into M(P)³−M(P)−1≥0. The increasing cubic on [1,∞) gives the parent’s sharp bound. No equality classification or isolated-spectrum theorem is added.

sources.match: The integral quotient and the two coefficient cases produce the nonreciprocal lower bound.

acceptance: The reciprocal polynomial X²−3X+1 is excluded even though its factorization exists.
The target inherits the precise short-gap verification gap; it is not marked closed.

nodes.title: Finite Fekete diameters and transfinite diameter
nodes.statement: For a compact K⊆ℂ and n≥2, δ_n(K)=sup_(z∈K^n) (∏_(0≤i<j<n)|z_i−z_j|)^(2/(n(n−1))). Set δ_n(∅)=0, δ_0=δ_1=0. Define d(K)=inf_(n≥2) δ_n(K). This d is the transfinite diameter, with the usual length normalization for logarithmic capacity. Only compact sets receive mathematical assertions.
hypotheses: K compact for the API. The total real-valued formula on other sets has no specified meaning.
Repeated tuple entries are permitted; a collision gives product zero. The infimum excludes indices 0 and 1.
proofSteps: For nonempty K, continuity on compact K^n gives a maximizing Fekete tuple and a finite nonnegative supremum. Define the empty-set values explicitly.
Use the nonnegative real power with exponent 2/(n(n−1)). The monotonicity and limit are separate theorem targets, rather than assumptions in the definition.

sources.match: The pairwise-distance supremum defines the finite diameter; its limit is monotone under inclusion and scales like length.
The transfinite diameter is the decreasing limit of the Fekete diameters and agrees with logarithmic capacity.

acceptance: δ_2 is the ordinary diameter, while d is typically smaller.

nodes.statement: For compact K⊆ℂ, let ‖p‖_K=sup_(z∈K)|p(z)|, with empty-set value 0. For n∈ℕ let t_n(K)=inf{‖p‖_K : p∈ℂ[X], p monic of degree n}. For nonempty K, t_0(K)=1. For n≥1, set T_n(K)=t_n(K)^(1/n). Minimizers need not be chosen canonically or claimed unique.
hypotheses: K compact; degree means natDegree together with monicity.
proofSteps: Bound the evaluation norm by compactness. The class of monic degree-n polynomials is nonempty, so its nonnegative norm infimum is finite.

For existence of a minimizer, if K has at most n points use its annihilating polynomial with a monic padding factor. Otherwise evaluation at n+1 distinct points bounds the coefficients of a norm-bounded minimizing sequence by Vandermonde inversion; take a convergent subsequence.

nodes.title: Fekete–Chebyshev equality and elementary diameter values
nodes.statement: For nonempty compact K, δ_n(K) decreases for n≥2 and tends to d(K). Also T_n(K) tends to d(K), and d(K)=inf_(n≥1) T_n(K). For R≥0, d(closedBall(b,R))=R. For a,b∈ℂ, d([a,b])=|b−a|/4. Finite sets have d=0.
hypotheses: K compact and nonempty for the convergence assertions; the empty-set convention is handled separately.
proofSteps: Delete each point in a maximizing tuple and multiply the resulting pair-product inequalities to prove δ_(n+1)≤δ_n.
Use submultiplicativity of t_n and the elementary subadditive limit argument (including a zero t_n) to identify the nth-root limit with its infimum.

Removing one point of a Fekete tuple provides a monic degree-n polynomial with norm at most δ_(n+1)^n. Conversely replace the monomials in a Vandermonde determinant by monic Chebyshev polynomials and use its permutation sum: δ_(n+1)^(n(n+1)/2)≤(n+1)!∏_(j=1)^n t_j. Taking logarithms and Cesàro means gives the reverse limit comparison; the zero-capacity case follows by approximation.

The circle gives t_n=R^n by the Cauchy coefficient bound and X^n. On [−1,1], the classical real Chebyshev polynomial has leading coefficient 2^(n−1) and alternating extrema; real parts rule out a better complex monic polynomial. Thus t_n=2^(1−n), and affine transport gives the segment value.

nodes.title: Transfinite diameter under a monic polynomial inverse image
nodes.statement: If K⊆ℂ is nonempty compact and P∈ℂ[X] is monic of degree m≥1, then P⁻¹(K) is nonempty compact and d(P⁻¹(K))=d(K)^(1/m). In particular d({z: |P(z)|≤r^m})=r for r≥0.
hypotheses: P monic and m≥1; inverse image means P(z)∈K, an existential membership condition.
proofSteps: A positive-degree polynomial is proper and surjective on ℂ, so its inverse image is compact and nonempty.
Pull back a monic degree-n Chebyshev polynomial on K to obtain t_(mn)(P⁻¹K)≤t_n(K).

For a monic degree-j Q on P⁻¹K, form its polynomial norm N_Q(y)=∏_(P(z)=y)Q(z), with root multiplicities. The resultant construction gives a monic polynomial in y of degree j after its harmless sign normalization, and |N_Q(y)|≤‖Q‖_(P⁻¹K)^m. Hence t_j(K)≤t_j(P⁻¹K)^m.
Apply the Fekete–Chebyshev limit to both inequalities. This proof uses a determinant norm, rather than assuming an unplanned equilibrium measure.

nodes.title: A regular lemniscate enclosing a compact set
nodes.statement: Given nonempty compact K⊆ℂ and r>d(K), there exist m≥1, a monic degree-m P, and ρ with d(K)<ρ<r such that ‖P‖_K<ρ^m and L={z:|P(z)|≤ρ^m} contains K in its interior. The level ρ^m avoids the absolute values of the nonzero critical values of P; ∂L is a finite union of smooth analytic closed curves, positively oriented with total winding number 1 about every point of L°. Also d(L)=ρ<r. For every j≥0 there is a monic degree-j Q_j and a constant C independent of j such that ‖Q_j‖_L≤Cρ^j.
hypotheses: r>d(K)≥0 implies r>0. No positive-capacity assumption on K is imposed.
The enclosure is not asserted to lie in an arbitrarily small Euclidean neighbourhood of K; holes may be filled.
proofSteps: Choose a degree m with t_m(K)^(1/m)<r and a monic P attaining that norm. Choose ρ strictly between its norm root and r, and above d(K), avoiding finitely many critical-value radii.

Properness and regularity of the polynomial level set give the compact enclosure, the strict interior inclusion and its finite analytic boundary. Apply the monic inverse-image formula to the radius-ρ^m disc.
For j=qm+s, 0≤s<m, use Q_j=P^q X^s. On L its norm is at most ρ^(mq) max_(z∈L)|z|^s; take C=max_(0≤s<m) max(1,max_(z∈L)|z|^s ρ^(−s)).

nodes.title: Conformal radius using the existing normalized map
nodes.statement: For a proper simply connected open Ω⊆ℂ and p∈Ω, take any existing TauCeti.IsNormalizedRiemannMapOn φ Ω p and define cr(Ω,p)=1/|φ′(p)|>0. The pinned existence and on-domain uniqueness theorems make this independent of φ. Outside the eligible pointed-domain class use value 0. No second normalized-map predicate or Riemann-map construction is introduced.
hypotheses: Ω is nonempty, open, simply connected and proper; p is a specified point of Ω.
Derivative positivity means its imaginary part is zero and its real part is strictly positive.
proofSteps: Use the pinned exists_isNormalizedRiemannMapOn; its derivative is a positive real number. On-domain uniqueness from IsNormalizedRiemannMapOn.eqOn implies equality of derivatives at p and hence equality of the reciprocal moduli.
Apply Schwarz’s derivative bound to the composition of two maps and their inverses to prove conformal-radius monotonicity under inclusion.

The affine coordinate change z↦az+b gives cr(aΩ+b,ap+b)=|a|cr(Ω,p) for a≠0. For an increasing open exhaustion, the inverse image of a closed radius-q disc is compact; it lies in one exhausting domain and gives the lower bound q·cr(Ω,p).

nodes.title: Dirichlet capacity for radial slit condensers
nodes.statement: For closed disjoint plates E₀,E₁⊆ℂ, with E₁ compact, positive separation, and G=ℂ∖(E₀∪E₁) bounded with finitely many analytic boundary arcs, define Cap_D(E₀,E₁)=inf_u ∫_G |∇u|² dA. Admissible u are continuous on ℂ, take values in [0,1], equal 0 on E₀ and 1 on E₁, are locally Lipschitz on G and C¹ off finitely many piecewise C¹ cuts, and have finite energy. The energy is the nonnegative extended integral of the squared real derivative norm; the infimum of an empty admissible class is +∞. The norm of the real Fréchet derivative ℂ→ℝ equals the Euclidean gradient norm.
hypotheses: This part uses E₀=ℂ∖D, E₁=closedBall(0,ε), where D is a disc with finitely many radial slits and 0<ε below the slit tips.
The area measure is Lebesgue measure on ℝ² transported by ℂ≃ℝ². No factor 1/(2π) is inserted.
Local Lipschitz regularity is imposed only in G, so gradients can be unbounded near slit endpoints on a plate.
proofSteps: Use an infimum in ℝ≥0∞ of nonnegative integrals; totalized real integrals of a nonintegrable function must not silently give zero.

The finite cuts have area zero, so changing derivative values on them does not affect energy. Radial logarithmic test functions give a nonempty class for round annuli; the special slit-domain comparisons use conformal pullbacks and monotonicity.
Do not introduce a general Sobolev-space, Perron-solution or harmonic-measure construction: the stated elementary variational class suffices for the source argument.

nodes.title: Dirichlet conformal invariance and the annulus formula
nodes.statement: For the radial slit condenser class, Cap_D is invariant under eligible conformal changes of coordinates. For round plates E₀={|z|≥R}, E₁={|z|≤r}, 0<r<R, Cap_D=2π/log(R/r). Plate monotonicity holds with the direction stated in the definition.
hypotheses: Coordinate maps are biholomorphisms of the open condenser domains with continuous corresponding boundary values; the composed tests remain in the prescribed class.
proofSteps: For a holomorphic conformal map the derivative multiplies real lengths by |φ′| and area by |φ′|². The chain rule and change of variables cancel the factors in the nonnegative Dirichlet integral; apply both map directions.

For an annulus, the admissible radial function log(R/|z|)/log(R/r) has energy 2π/log(R/r). On each radial line, the endpoint value difference is 1; weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives radial energy at least 1/log(R/r). Integrate angles and discard the nonnegative angular contribution.
The larger-plate admissible class is a subset of the smaller-plate class, and gradients vanish in the plate regions. This proves monotonicity.

nodes.title: The small-inner-disc capacity asymptotic
nodes.statement: Let D be a bounded simply connected radial slit disc containing 0, and c_D=cr(D,0). For 0<ε sufficiently small put C_D(ε)=Cap_D(ℂ∖D,closedBall(0,ε)). Then 2π/C_D(ε)=log(1/ε)+log(c_D)+o(1) as ε→0+. In particular C_D(ε)≤C_E(ε) for all sufficiently small ε implies cr(D,0)≥cr(E,0).
hypotheses: D and E have the specified finite slit geometry and contain 0. Capacity is finite and positive for these separated plates.
proofSteps: Use the normalized Riemann map φ with φ′(0)=1/c_D. Its image of the small inner disc is sandwiched between concentric discs of radii ε/c_D·(1±o(1)), from uniform differentiability and the inverse-map expansion.

Conformal invariance and plate monotonicity sandwich the capacity between the two explicit annulus capacities. Taking reciprocals yields the asserted asymptotic with the plus sign in front of log(c_D).
For the comparison, take reciprocal capacities, subtract log(1/ε), and pass to the limit.

nodes.title: Dubinin’s finite rotational desymmetrization
nodes.statement: For n≥1 distinct ray directions θ_j and 0<r<1, let D(r;θ)=ball(0,1)∖⋃_j{t exp(iθ_j):r≤t<1}. Let D*(r,n) use equally spaced directions 2πj/n. There is a finite partition into angular pieces with rotations about 0 sending the regular slit configuration to the prescribed one. On identified cut boundaries, the inverse images differ by elements of the dihedral symmetry group of the regular configuration. Consequently every dihedrally invariant admissible test function on D* transfers to a continuous admissible test function on D with the same Dirichlet energy and unchanged circular inner and outer plate values.
hypotheses: Distinct directions and positive slit tip radius; repeated rays are collapsed before applying this construction.
A partition of the plane into closed angular pieces has disjoint interiors; energy is computed on those interiors, and finite cuts have area zero.
proofSteps: Use the angle-subdivision construction in Dubinin Lemma 1: move sectors by rotations, split a sector at every mismatch, and match cut rays by the dihedral reflections. The finite procedure reduces the remaining unmatched angular pieces.

Define the transferred function on each rotated piece by composing the original function with the inverse rotation. Dihedral invariance gives equal values on common cuts. Lemma 2 supplies local Lipschitz regularity across them; finite C1 cuts are transported to finite C1 cuts.

Rotations have area Jacobian 1 and preserve the gradient norm, so the sum of piece energies is unchanged. Rotations preserve the concentric plate circles and send the regular slits to the prescribed slit plate.

nodes.title: Transfinite diameter and the inverted exterior radius
nodes.statement: Let K be a nontrivial finite radial hedgehog and b>0. Put U_b={0}∪{b/z:z∈ℂ∖K}. Then U_b is a proper simply connected open domain containing 0 and d(K)=b/cr(U_b,0). Equivalently the normalized exterior map Ψ:ℂ∖K→{|w|>1} has Ψ(z)=γz+O(1) at infinity with γ=1/d(K)>0.
hypotheses: Nontrivial means K contains a nonzero endpoint; the singleton hedgehog has d=0 and its inverted domain is the entire plane, which has no disc Riemann map.
proofSteps: The inverted domain is the plane with finitely many outward rays deleted, hence is open and star-convex at 0. Use the pinned contractibility and Riemann-mapping results. Invert its normalized map to obtain Ψ(z)=1/φ(b/z), with γ=φ′(0)/b.

For r>1 the level curve Γ_r=Ψ⁻¹({|w|=r}) encloses K. The polynomial part Q_n of γ⁻ⁿΨⁿ is monic of degree n. Its Cauchy contour representation gives ‖Q_n‖_K≤C_r(r/γ)^n. The Chebyshev limit gives d(K)≤1/γ as r decreases to 1.

For every monic degree-n p, p/Ψⁿ is holomorphic on the exterior, including infinity, and tends to γ⁻ⁿ there. The maximum principle on the exterior of Γ_r yields γ⁻ⁿ≤r⁻ⁿ‖p‖_(Γ_r). The curves approach K as r decreases to 1, yielding ‖p‖_K≥γ⁻ⁿ. Take the Chebyshev limit for the reverse inequality.

sources.locator: §3, Theorem 3.5 and Example 3.6, p. 185; §1, Theorem 1.9, pp. 172–173
sources.match: The leading coefficient of the exterior conformal map is the reciprocal capacity, and capacity equals the transfinite diameter. The displayed proof uses the already planned Chebyshev characterization instead of adding a general energy-minimization theory.

acceptance: For [0,a], the exterior radius relation gives d=|a|/4. The scale b is retained explicitly; taking b=R in the hedgehog comparison avoids a reciprocal-scale error.

nodes.title: Dubinin’s radial hedgehog bound
nodes.statement: For n≥1 and endpoints a₁,…,a_n∈ℂ, with R=max_i|a_i|, d(K(a))≤R·4^(−1/n). Equivalently d(K(a))^n≤R^n/4. Zero endpoints, repeated endpoints and coincident rays are allowed. For the regular n-spike hedgehog with endpoints R exp(2πij/n), equality holds.
hypotheses: n≥1; the bound is interpreted with the usual positive real nth root.
proofSteps: If R=0 then K={0} and its diameter is zero. Otherwise extend every nonzero segment to length R, collapse coincident rays, and let m≤n be the resulting positive number of distinct rays. Monotonicity reduces to this equal-length hedgehog.

Invert by z↦R/z. The resulting domain U is the plane minus m outward rays starting on the unit circle. Exhaust it by U∩ball(0,L), L>1. Scaling by 1/L gives the slit discs with tip radius 1/L. Dubinin’s slit-radius comparison and conformal-radius exhaustion give cr(U,0)≥cr(U*,0).

Apply the exterior-radius identity to turn this into d(K)≤d(K*). The regular m-spike set is the inverse image of [0,R^m] under X^m, so the monic inverse-image formula and d([0,s])=s/4 give d(K*)=R4^(−1/m)≤R4^(−1/n).

sources.match: Dubinin’s bound for a finite union of radial segments is the analytic inequality needed by Schinzel–Zassenhaus.
The normalized slit-map derivative comparison supplies the geometric inequality through inversion and exhaustion.

acceptance: One endpoint a gives the sharp value |a|/4. Endpoints 1,−1 give the sharp value 1/2. Endpoints 1,1 give 1/4, strictly below the n=2 bound 1/2; multiplicity is not an equality hypothesis.

nodes.title: The shifted leading Hankel determinant
nodes.statement: For a sequence a:ℕ→R over a commutative ring and n∈ℕ, H_n(a) is the n×n matrix with entry a_(i+j+1), 0≤i,j<n, and D_n(a)=det H_n(a). In particular D₀=1. The coefficient a₀ does not enter these determinants.
hypotheses: The +1 shift corresponds to the Laurent coefficient extracted by ∮G(z)z^k dz; use this convention throughout.
proofSteps: Use Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R and the existing determinant. Ring-hom compatibility follows from determinant naturality.
A tail recurrence makes sufficiently many columns dependent, while the exact converse needs eventual vanishing of every leading determinant, as in Kronecker’s criterion.

sources.locator: §4, Hankel determinant in the proof of Theorem 4, pp. 13–14
sources.match: The matrix uses the coefficient shift a_(i+j+1).
Kronecker’s criterion is written for the unshifted sequence; apply it to the tail a_(j+1).

acceptance: A single zero leading determinant does not establish rationality.

nodes.title: An exterior Laurent continuation
nodes.statement: For a:ℕ→ℂ and compact nonempty K⊆ℂ, an exterior Laurent continuation is a function G:ℂ→ℂ holomorphic on ℂ∖K, together with R>0 such that K⊆closedBall(0,R) and, whenever |z|>R, HasSum(Σ_j a_j z^(−j),G(z)). Equivalently the summand is a_j(z⁻¹)^j. Values of G on K are irrelevant.
hypotheses: Only a convergent germ at infinity is claimed; arbitrary formal series are not silently treated as analytic functions.
Connectedness of ℂ∖K is not required for the formal rationality conclusion. If the conclusion also identifies G with the rational function everywhere off K, require connectedness.
proofSteps: Store an unbundled holomorphic witness and an exterior convergence radius. The radius can be enlarged, and the excluded compact set can be enlarged, without changing the germ.
On a connected complement the identity theorem makes the witness unique there. The formal series at infinity is PowerSeries.mk a in the variable w=1/z.

sources.match: A convergent integer Laurent germ extends as a single-valued holomorphic function outside a small-diameter compact set.
The extension assumption is imposed on the germ, not merely on an unrelated holomorphic function.

acceptance: A0 may be nonzero. It is a constant term and has no effect on the shifted Hankel rationality criterion.

api.name: exteriorContinuation_enlarge_radius
api.statement: Any larger positive radius containing K is a valid convergence radius.

api.name: exteriorContinuation_enlarge_set
api.statement: If K⊆L are compact, restrict the same witness to ℂ∖L and enlarge its radius.

api.name: exteriorContinuation_unique
api.statement: For connected ℂ∖K, two witnesses for the same coefficients agree off K.

api.name: exteriorContinuation_coeff

api.name: exteriorContinuation_moment

Records the single-valued square-root branch with its actual formal germ.

nodes.title: Kronecker’s eventual Hankel vanishing criterion
nodes.statement: For a sequence a over a field k, PowerSeries.mk a is rational in the sense of CA.2/rational-power-series if and only if there exists N such that D_n(a)=0 for all n≥N. The denominator may be normalized to have constant term 1; no degree bound on the numerator is assumed.
hypotheses: k is a field; no characteristic-zero hypothesis is needed for this algebraic criterion.
proofSteps: Rationality gives a linear recurrence for the coefficients after the numerator degree. For large n its shifted moment matrix has dependent columns, and D_n=0.

Conversely apply the source criterion to the tail b_j=a_(j+1). If all its leading determinants vanish, its first nonzero coefficient would give a nonzero anti-diagonal determinant, so the tail is zero. Otherwise take r maximal with a nonzero r×r leading determinant. Solve the unique r-term recurrence from its invertible block.

If the first later recurrence failure is at the index controlled by d≥0, a block determinant factors as det(A_r) times a nonzero anti-diagonal block of size d+1, with sign (−1)^((d+1)d/2). This contradicts maximality. The recurrence is therefore valid from a finite index onward. Multiply the series by its recurrence polynomial to get a polynomial; adding a₀ does not change rationality.

sources.match: Eventual vanishing of all leading Hankel determinants characterizes rational formal series. The proof is used with the sign, index and recurrence corrections recorded under sourceIssues.
Kronecker’s determinant criterion links rationality to eventual determinant vanishing.

acceptance: The +1 shift discards only the constant coefficient. A zero determinant at one size does not satisfy the eventual condition.

nodes.title: Analytic n²-growth bound for Hankel determinants
nodes.statement: If a has an exterior Laurent continuation outside a nonempty compact K, then for every r>d(K) there exists B>0 such that |D_n(a)|≤n! B^n r^(n(n−1)) for every n∈ℕ. In particular limsup_(n→∞)|D_n(a)|^(1/n²)≤d(K).
hypotheses: r>d(K)≥0, so r>0. The limsup statement concerns n≥1.
proofSteps: Choose a regular lemniscate enclosure L of diameter ρ with d(K)<ρ<r. Its boundary Γ lies off K and encloses K. The Laurent coefficient formula gives a_(k+1)=(2πi)⁻¹∮_ΓG(z)z^k dz, by deforming a large coefficient circle through the holomorphy region.

Change rows and columns from X^i to the monic basis Q_i supplied by the enclosure. Both change-of-basis matrices are triangular with diagonal 1, so their determinants are 1. The new moment entries obey |L(Q_iQ_j)|≤Bρ^(i+j), with B independent of i,j.

The determinant expansion has n! terms; in every term Σ_i(i+σ(i))=n(n−1). This gives the stated bound (enlarge B if needed and use ρ<r). Take n²th roots; log(n!)/n² and log(B)/n tend to zero, then let r decrease to d(K).

sources.match: Contour coefficient formulas and Chebyshev estimates give the quadratic-exponent determinant bound.
Monic row and column transformations expose the capacity bound on Hankel determinants.

acceptance: At n=0 both sides equal 1. Factorial growth is negligible relative to any fixed r^(n²) with r<1; no unjustified uniform bound in n is imposed on G’s raw coefficients.

nodes.title: Bertrandias’s integer Laurent rationality criterion
nodes.statement: Let a:ℕ→ℤ, and suppose its complex coefficient casts have an exterior Laurent continuation outside a nonempty compact K⊆ℂ with d(K)<1. Then PowerSeries.mk (a cast to ℚ) is rational: there exist P,Q∈ℚ[X] with Q(0)≠0 and Q·PowerSeries.mk a=P in ℚ⟦X⟧. If ℂ∖K is connected, the continuation agrees there with that rational germ wherever its expression in 1/z is defined.
hypotheses: Integer coefficients and the strict diameter bound are essential. The main conclusion is rationality over ℚ, not a claim that every allowed denominator has integer constant term ±1.
proofSteps: Choose d(K)<r<1. The analytic estimate gives |D_n|≤n!B^n r^(n(n−1)), which tends to zero because its logarithm has a negative quadratic leading term.

Each complex determinant is the cast of an integer determinant. For sufficiently large n its norm is below 1, so the integer determinant is zero. Transfer zero to ℚ and apply Kronecker’s criterion over ℚ.
On a connected complement, the identity theorem extends the equality of the rational germ and G away from poles and z=0; removable points are interpreted through G.

sources.match: The archimedean small-diameter continuation condition forces integer Hankel determinants to vanish.
The integer-coefficient specialization is the rationality input used for the square root.

acceptance: The criterion applies to K={2} of diameter 0 for G=1/(z−2), despite a finite pole. K=[0,1] has diameter 1/4, but the normalized square-root example is excluded by its noninteger coefficients.

nodes.title: The square-root branch outside a hedgehog
nodes.statement: For a nonempty finite endpoint family β_i∈ℂ, put K=K(β) and Q(w)=∏_i(1−β_i w). There is a unique complex formal series S with S(0)=1 and S²=Q. Off K define G(z)=∏_i exp((1/2)log(1−β_i/z)), using the principal log. Then G is holomorphic off K, G(z)²=Q(1/z), G tends to 1 at infinity, and G is an exterior Laurent continuation of the coefficients of S.
hypotheses: 0∈K, so z⁻¹ is well-defined at every point of the holomorphy domain. Zero and repeated β_i are allowed.
This statement produces a complex series; integer coefficients must be supplied separately by CA.6/integral-square-root-power-series.
proofSteps: If z∉[0,β_i], then 1−β_i/z avoids the nonpositive real ray. Indeed a nonpositive real value would make z a real multiple tβ_i with 0<t≤1. Thus each principal-log factor is holomorphic outside K, and exp(log u)=u gives its square.

For |z| larger than every |β_i| the usual normalized analytic square root has a convergent expansion at infinity. The coefficient recursion 2s_m=q_m−Σ_(0<j<m)s_js_(m−j) uniquely specifies S over ℂ. Hence the analytic branch and the formal normalized square root have identical coefficients.
Multiply finitely many factors. Every factor tends to 1 at infinity; this fixes the sign of the square root.

sources.match: The cuts join 0 to the roots of P₂ and P₄, making the normalized square root single-valued outside their hedgehog.

acceptance: No free choice of signs on separate factors is allowed: the value at infinity is 1.

nodes.title: The capacity-to-rationality input of Dimitrov’s bound
nodes.statement: For n≥1, endpoints β₁,…,β_n, and an integer formal series S with S(0)=1 and S²=∏_i(1−β_i w) after casting to ℂ, if R=max_i|β_i| satisfies R^n<4, then S is rational over ℚ. In the parent Schinzel–Zassenhaus argument use β=(α_i²,α_i⁴), n=2d: if the house H>1 obeys H<2^(1/(4d)), then R≤H⁴ and R^(2d)<4, so this theorem makes the parent’s normalized integral square root rational.
hypotheses: The integer square-root hypothesis is explicit and supplied by the existing parent construction. The displayed house substitution concerns the unit case H>1 used in the parent degree induction.
proofSteps: The hedgehog square-root construction gives the exterior continuation of the integer coefficient casts. Dubinin’s bound and R^n<4 imply d(K)<1. Apply Bertrandias’s rationality criterion.

For a rational square root S of a polynomial, every irreducible factor of that polynomial has even valuation. The normalized reciprocal root product therefore corresponds to a square product P₂P₄ in the parent algebraic argument.
Bind this analytic result to the existing parent degree induction and corrected square-cyclotomic criterion; do not introduce a second Schinzel–Zassenhaus target.

sources.locator: §4, proof of Theorem 1, pp. 15–16, after Corollary 5

acceptance: For d=1 the threshold in the contradiction is H<2^(1/4), and the estimate uses 2d segments, not d. A rational square-root branch does not alone prove cyclotomicity; the parent arithmetic induction is required.
